•  Effective spatial resolution lower than nominal: Each 10?m pixel effectively reflects the largest canopy-top height within a ~25?m GEDI footprint, reducing the ability to resolve individual vegetation features.
•  Sparse supervision and geolocation errors: Limited GEDI coverage and 15–20?m geolocation uncertainty obscure fine-scale canopy height variations and introduce noise between adjacent pixels.
•  Tiling artifacts and systematic offsets: Tile borders, especially at high latitudes, show inconsistencies, potentially degrading absolute height estimates for locally unique vegetation structures.
•  Overestimation in low-canopy areas: Canopy heights under 5?m tend to be overestimated, despite accurate tall canopy mapping.
•  Persistent cloud cover artifacts: Minor map artifacts occur in regions with high cloud frequency.
•  High predictive uncertainty in specific regions: Tropical areas (e.g., Papua New Guinea) and northern latitudes (e.g., Alaska) exhibit high uncertainty.
•  Optical-only limitations: Reliance solely on optical imagery constrains the accuracy of canopy height estimation, suggesting the need for integrating additional environmental predictors.
•  Potential for future improvement: Super-resolution methods, updated GEDI versions, and uncertainty-based filtering could enhance small-feature preservation and reduce biased estimates.

column16: The classification integrates multi-source features from optical, radar, climatic, and spatial data. Sentinel-2 inputs are temporally composited and summarized using percentile statistics, with data quality controlled through the Land Occlusion Score (LOS), which models clouds, shadows, snow, and surface probabilities. Sentinel-1 backscatter (VV, VH, and their ratio) is likewise aggregated into percentile-based temporal metrics. Climatic variables from AgERA5 are summarized and reduced into low-dimensional embeddings using UMAP to capture regional meteorological patterns. Additional spatial features, including geographic coordinates and elevation, provide contextual information, allowing the model to combine spectral, structural, climatic, and locational signals within a unified classification framework.
column17: EvoNet based land cover model training and global inference (algorithm method that combines the advantages of CNNs with traditional pixel-based classifiers within a single integrated framework)
column19:
The training dataset consists of over 45,000 image patches, each measuring 1280 × 1280 m², sampled globally using a heterogeneity-based strategy.

A class-balanced subset of these ~45,000 patches was used to train the AI model, while a separate independent subset was reserved for global validation.
column20: The validation followed a blind, probability-based response design in which 1-hectare spatial assessment units (containing 100 pixels of 10 m × 10 m) were interpreted independently of the map’s predicted classes. Each pixel within the hectare was assigned a reference land-cover code according to the product’s class definitions, using both the pixel-level signal and surrounding contextual information to support consistent interpretation. Validation was conducted on the native LCM-10 product in its original UTM projection to ensure perfect spatial alignment with Sentinel-2 pixels and equal-area assessment globally, thereby avoiding distortions or resampling errors from reprojection. This design enabled the estimation of class-specific omission and commission errors at a standardized spatial unit.

column22: The accuracy assessment used 10,702 validation samples (1 ha each) for continental, biome, and country-level metrics, and a double-interpreted subset of 1,070 samples (overlapping with the larger set) to compute the global accuracy metrics.

column26: Most land-cover classes met or exceeded target performance levels. However, some class-specific weaknesses were identified through user’s and producer’s accuracy metrics and analysis of the confusion matrices. Grassland (class 30) and Herbaceous Wetland (class 50) exhibited low producer’s accuracy, indicating omission errors. Moss and Lichen (class 70) and Built-up areas (class 90) showed low user’s accuracy, reflecting commission errors. Shrubland (class 20) was the only class with low performance in both user’s and producer’s accuracy, suggesting both omission and commission issues.
